blocks.text: 1. Reflection

blocks.alt: An action produces a result, which goes through self-evaluation

blocks.text: Planning closed by naming itself and reflection as complementary halves of a full agentic loop. Reflection, an agent evaluating its own results after acting, is that second half, closing the gap between simply acting and actually verifying the action worked.
It checks whether a completed step actually achieved what it was meant to before moving on.
2. Acting Versus Evaluating The Result
Executing a tool call, the step covered in Tool Calling, is only half the loop: it produces a raw result.
Reflection is the other half, judging whether that raw result is actually good enough.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Phase","What it produces"],"rows":[["Acting","A raw result from executing a tool call"],["Reflection","A judgment of whether that result is good enough"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Comparing The Result Against The Original Goal

blocks.alt: A result is compared against the original goal

blocks.text: Reflection measures a step's output against what the original goal actually needed, much like how Self-RAG scores overall response quality.
A technically successful call can still fail to serve the goal.
4. Detecting A Failed Or Insufficient Step

blocks.alt: A step result is checked for being sufficient

blocks.text: Reflection is what actually catches a bad or incomplete result before it silently propagates forward, much like how an error in an early hop propagates forward in Multi-Hop RAG.
Without it, a flawed step simply continues on to the next stage unnoticed.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A tool call that returns an empty or clearly wrong result would silently continue to the next step without reflection, the same propagation risk as an error in an early hop.

blocks.text: 5. Deciding To Retry Or Revise A Failed Step

blocks.alt: A failed step is decided to retry or revise

blocks.text: Once a step is judged insufficient, the agent can retry it, try a different tool, or revise the plan.
Reflection feeds directly back into planning to correct course.
6. Reflection On The Final Answer Too
Reflection applies not just per step but also to the complete final answer before it is returned, the same idea behind reflecting on retrieved passage relevance in Self-RAG.
It is a last check that the overall goal was actually satisfied.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Reflection scope","What it checks"],"rows":[["Per-step reflection","Whether one completed step achieved its purpose"],["Final answer reflection","Whether the overall goal was actually satisfied"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Reflection Requires A Critic, Not Just Execution

blocks.alt: Execution only is compared against execution plus a critic

blocks.text: Judging a result well requires a separate evaluative pass, not just running the next step, similar to how the grader is its own small model in Corrective RAG.
That evaluative pass can itself be a smaller, dedicated model or prompt.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A dedicated critic prompt or smaller model asked specifically to judge a step's result is a separate evaluative pass, distinct from the model that generated the result being judged.

blocks.text: 8. Reflection Adds An Extra Call Per Step
Evaluating every single step's result means an added call on top of the step itself, the same latency tradeoff behind each added step costing latency in Advanced RAG.
It is a real cost that scales with how many steps the plan actually has.
9. Recognizing When Reflection Earns Its Added Evaluation Cost

blocks.alt: High-stakes actions point toward using reflection

blocks.text: Multi-step tasks where an early error would be costly justify reflection.
A single, reliable tool call, by contrast, rarely needs a dedicated reflection pass.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Executing every step without ever checking whether the result actually satisfies the goal.
Judging a result as successful just because the tool call itself did not error out.
Using the same model pass for both generating and evaluating a result with no separate check.
Adding per-step reflection to a workflow with only one simple, highly reliable tool call.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Reflection is an agent evaluating its own results after acting, not just executing steps.
Executing a tool call produces a raw result; reflection judges whether it is good enough.
Reflection measures a step's output against what the original goal actually needed.
Reflection catches a bad or incomplete result before it silently propagates forward.
A step judged insufficient can be retried, tried with a different tool, or replanned.
Reflection applies to the complete final answer too, not just each individual step.
Judging a result well requires a separate evaluative pass, often a dedicated critic model.
Evaluating every step adds its own call, a real cost scaling with the number of steps.
